cards.statement: The C# compiler translates LINQ query syntax into calls to query-operator methods.
cards.explanation: Query clauses map to method calls during compilation. In LINQ to Objects, those calls use the query operators supplied by Enumerable.

cards.statement: Enumerating `new[] { -2, 3 }.Where(n => n > 0)` yields the original source value 3.
cards.explanation: Enumerable.Where yields input elements that pass its predicate. In this query, 3 passes the positive-value test.

cards.statement: For `IEnumerable<string> words`, `words.Select(w => w.Length)` produces `IEnumerable<string>`.
cards.explanation: The projection Select(w => w.Length) produces an IEnumerable<int>. Its selector returns an int for a source string.
cards.misconception: Enumerable.Select preserves the source element type even when the selector produces a different type.

cards.statement: For `IEnumerable<int[]> groups`, `groups.SelectMany(g => g)` yields individual integers.
cards.explanation: Enumerable.SelectMany enumerates the sequences produced by its selector and combines their elements into one output sequence.

cards.statement: For a nonempty `int[] source`, `source.Any(Test)` can return before it calls the Test predicate.
cards.explanation: For a nonempty source, Any(Test) calls the predicate during the Any call to determine its Boolean result. The query executes immediately.
cards.misconception: Any postpones predicate evaluation until a later enumeration.

cards.statement: Calling `Enumerable.First` on an empty `IEnumerable<int>` returns the default value 0.
cards.explanation: Enumerable.First throws InvalidOperationException when its source sequence is empty.
cards.misconception: Enumerable.First supplies default(T) when the sequence has no elements.

cards.statement: `new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.Single(x => x == 2)` throws because its source contains several elements.
cards.explanation: Single's predicate overload requires exactly one match. `new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.Single(x => x == 2)` returns 2.
cards.misconception: The predicate overload of Single requires the entire source to contain exactly one element.

cards.statement: Re-enumerating a deferred `Where` query over a `List<int>` uses the list's current elements.
cards.explanation: A deferred LINQ query reads source data when it executes. A later enumeration evaluates the query against the source's data at that time.

cards.statement: During `foreach`, LINQ to Objects `OrderBy` yields sorted values while it continues consuming its source.
cards.explanation: OrderBy and GroupBy buffer source data when enumeration begins. During ordinary enumeration, they finish reading the source before yielding the first result.
cards.misconception: Deferred sorting produces output incrementally while it reads the source.

cards.statement: For a `List<T> list`, `Enumerable.Count(list)` can obtain its result from the list's `Count` property.
cards.explanation: Enumerable.Count obtains the count from an ICollection<T> implementation such as List<T>, avoiding element-by-element enumeration.

cards.statement: Calling `ToList()` on a LINQ query computes and stores its result elements during that call.
cards.explanation: The returned List<T> holds materialized query results. Iterating that list reuses its stored elements instead of executing the original query again.

cards.statement: Calling `OrderBy` again on an ordered LINQ to Objects sequence adds a secondary sort key.
cards.explanation: A second OrderBy establishes a new primary ordering. ThenBy adds a secondary key to an existing ordering.
cards.misconception: Chaining OrderBy preserves the earlier primary key and adds a secondary key like ThenBy.

cards.statement: A caller can pass an unassigned int local to a ref parameter when the callee assigns it.
cards.explanation: A ref argument must be definitely assigned before the call, even when the called method will assign it.
cards.misconception: A ref callee's assignment replaces caller definite assignment.

cards.statement: The compiler requires a method to assign its out int parameter before returning normally.
cards.explanation: The compiler checks that a method definitely assigns its out parameters before a normal return.

cards.statement: A method can replace an in int parameter's value with an assignment inside its body.
cards.explanation: An in parameter is read-only to the method; assigning a new value to it produces a compiler error.
cards.misconception: An in parameter permits reassignment by the callee.

cards.statement: C# evaluates named argument expressions in the order they appear at the call site.
cards.explanation: Named arguments change which parameter receives a value; their expressions still evaluate in written argument order.

cards.statement: For void Save(int retries = 3), calling Save() supplies the type default for retries.
cards.explanation: Calling Save() uses its declared retries default, 3, rather than default(int), which is 0.
cards.misconception: Omitted optional arguments use the parameter type's default.

cards.statement: In C# 13, a params Span<int> parameter accepts comma-separated int arguments at the call site.
cards.explanation: Span<T> is a supported params collection target; the compiler gathers the supplied elements for the call.

cards.statement: A caller can invoke an in-scope WordCount(this string s) extension as "hi".WordCount().
cards.explanation: Classic extension methods use a static declaration with this on the receiver parameter and retain instance-style call syntax.

cards.statement: Adding a project reference automatically brings that assembly's extension methods into scope.
cards.explanation: Instance-style extension calls need the declaring namespace in scope, commonly through a using directive.
cards.misconception: An assembly reference imports its extension methods.

cards.statement: C# selects an applicable instance method before a matching extension method of the same name.
cards.explanation: The compiler considers ordinary applicable members before searching for extension methods.

cards.statement: An extension-method call selects its overload from the receiver object's runtime type.
cards.explanation: The compiler binds an extension call using the receiver expression's compile-time type.
cards.misconception: Extension overloads dispatch from the receiver's runtime type.

cards.statement: Declaring an extension method grants it access to private members of the extended type.
cards.explanation: Extension methods follow the extended type's accessibility rules; the extension declaration grants no private access.
cards.misconception: Extension methods receive the extended type's private access.

cards.statement: In C# 14, an extension block for string supports a static property accessed as string.EmptyAlias.
cards.explanation: C# 14 extension blocks group instance or static extension methods and properties. A static property uses the extended type's name.

cards.statement: The compiler automatically binds Console.WriteLine to a compatible overload for an Action<string> assignment.
cards.explanation: The assignment converts the WriteLine method group into an Action<string> delegate. Its selected method takes a string and returns void.

cards.statement: Func<int, string> uses its first type argument to determine the delegate's return type.
cards.explanation: Func<int, string> returns a string. The final type argument specifies the result type.
cards.misconception: The first type argument of Func specifies its result type.

cards.statement: A normally completed multicast invocation calls its handlers in their invocation-list order.
cards.explanation: Combining delegates builds an ordered invocation list. An invocation calls the registered methods in that sequence.

cards.statement: A multicast Func<int> invocation that finishes normally returns the result from its first handler.
cards.explanation: When a multicast delegate returning a value finishes normally, its caller receives the last invoked method's return value.
cards.misconception: A multicast delegate exposes the return value from its first invoked method.

cards.statement: A lambda that captures an outer local freezes that local's value when creating its delegate.
cards.explanation: A captured local remains a shared variable. A later invocation observes its current value, including changes made after the delegate's creation.
cards.misconception: Lambda capture freezes the local's value at delegate creation.

cards.statement: A static lambda can capture an ordinary int local from the enclosing method.
cards.explanation: The static modifier rejects captures of enclosing locals and instance state. Pass a needed value as a lambda parameter.
cards.misconception: A static lambda admits outer-local capture when the local holds a value type.

cards.statement: C# 14 allows a lambda to use an inferred parameter type with an out modifier.
cards.explanation: A C# 14 lambda's out parameter gets its type from the target delegate even when the lambda omits the type name.

cards.statement: C# 14 allows a lambda parameter with params to infer its parameter type from the target delegate.
cards.explanation: The params modifier still needs an explicit parameter type in a C# 14 lambda. For example, declare params int[] values.
cards.misconception: The relaxed C# 14 lambda modifier syntax also admits implicitly typed params parameters.

cards.statement: A subscriber can use -= with its registered handler to unsubscribe from an accessible event.
cards.explanation: Subscriber code uses += to add a handler and -= to remove it. Preserve the subscribed delegate to remove an anonymous handler later.

source.title: How to subscribe to and unsubscribe from events

cards.statement: A delegate bound to a class instance's method retains the receiver chosen when the delegate is created.
cards.explanation: An instance-method delegate stores its method and target object. Invoking the delegate calls that method on the stored target.

cards.statement: A derived class directly invokes its base class's public event through the inherited event member.
cards.explanation: The event's declaring type holds invocation privilege. A derived class raises that inherited event through a base method that invokes it.
cards.misconception: Public accessibility grants a derived class direct invocation privilege over a base event.

source.title: How to raise base class events in derived classes

cards.statement: In C# 14, a partial event's implementing half supplies the add and remove accessor bodies.
cards.explanation: A partial event pairs a field-like defining declaration with an implementing declaration that contains its add and remove accessors.

cards.statement: Awaiting a successfully completed Task<int> produces a Task<int> value.
cards.explanation: Awaiting Task<int> produces the task's int result. The await expression unwraps the result value for the caller.
cards.misconception: Await returns another task rather than its result.

cards.statement: An ordinary async Task method executes its initial statements synchronously on the calling thread.
cards.explanation: An ordinary async Task method begins its body as part of the call. Its initial synchronous work happens before that call returns.

cards.statement: Awaiting an already completed Task lets the enclosing async method continue immediately.
cards.explanation: An already completed await operand makes await finish immediately. The enclosing async method proceeds without suspension.

cards.statement: The compiler issues a warning for `async Task M() { return; }`.
cards.explanation: This async Task method is valid C#. Its missing await triggers a warning, which the deck's build settings permit.

cards.statement: Calling an async Task method creates another thread to execute its method body.
cards.explanation: The async and await keywords arrange asynchronous control flow. They do not themselves create another thread.
cards.misconception: The async modifier launches a new thread.

cards.statement: Task.Run(Action) queues the supplied CPU work for execution on the thread pool.
cards.explanation: Task.Run(Action) places the delegate invocation on the thread pool and returns a Task representing that invocation.

cards.statement: Calling Wait() on a running Task lets the calling thread return while that task is incomplete.
cards.explanation: Task.Wait() blocks the calling thread until the running task completes. The caller stays inside Wait during that interval.
cards.misconception: Wait releases the calling thread while waiting.

cards.statement: Starting independent asynchronous operations before awaiting them allows their work to overlap.
cards.explanation: Start the operations and keep their tasks before awaiting results. The first wait then occurs after the independent work has already begun.

source.title: Asynchronous programming with async and await

cards.statement: Task.WhenAll(tasks) can finish when an input task faults while other tasks remain incomplete.
cards.explanation: The combined task reaches completion after the last input task finishes, even when some finish unsuccessfully.
cards.misconception: WhenAll stops waiting as soon as one input task fails.

cards.statement: After successful completion, Task.WhenAll<int>(tasks) orders its results by task completion time.
cards.explanation: Task.WhenAll<int> produces an int array in input-task order. A faster task keeps the result position assigned by its input position.
cards.misconception: WhenAll arranges results by completion time.

cards.statement: For initially incomplete tasks, awaiting Task.WhenAny(tasks) yields the first completed input Task.
cards.explanation: WhenAny's outer task completes when one input finishes. Awaiting it yields that completed input task itself.

cards.statement: Awaiting Task.WhenAny(tasks) propagates a fault from the winning input task to the caller.
cards.explanation: The outer WhenAny task completes successfully even when its winner faults. Await the returned input task to observe that failure.
cards.misconception: Awaiting WhenAny also observes the winning task's failure.
